summary: For 5-6 year olds, quantitative reasoning is a two-way translation between a real situation and a concrete/pictorial model: acting out 'five ducks and two more swim up' with cubes, AND going the other way — given cubes, telling a matching story. The heart (CCSS MP2) is attending to the MEANING of quantities, not just producing a total: knowing THIS cube stands for a duck, that 5 and 2 are the parts and the whole is the total, and that 'putting together' is what makes it addition. Taught through story-acting and the concrete→pictorial bridge NCETM describes for the youngest bar model: line objects up, stand a drawn bar beside them, and ask 'what's the same, what's different?' so the picture is understood as an abstraction of the real thing.
misconceptions: Treats the model as a picture of two separate amounts, not a relationship — lays out 5 and 2 but cannot say which is the whole or show the joining
Loses the exact quantities when telling a story from objects ('some ducks and some more') instead of preserving 5 and 2
Produces the total by counting all but cannot point to the parts or the action inside the model
Picks the operation from a word ('more' → add) rather than from what happens in the situation

activities.title: Build the story, then flip it
steps: Listen to or watch a short story: 'Five ducks bob on a pond, then two more paddle in.'
Drag/place five cubes into the left of a part-whole frame and two into the right to match the story.
Watch a bar form across the top and the sentence 5 + 2 = 7 appear, with the '5' marking the first cubes and the '2' marking the newcomers.
Point to which cubes are the 5, which are the 2, and show the whole group.

'Flip it': take a pile of cubes already split (e.g. 4 and 3) and invent a story the picture could tell — then notice the SAME cubes could be 'four birds and three more' OR 'seven birds, three flew off'.
activities.insight: The model carries meaning in both directions: numbers stand for ducks, the joining stands for adding, and the child can travel from world to symbol and back — the model is not a picture of an answer but a thing that holds a relationship.

activities.title: Line up, cubes, bar — what's the same, what's different?
steps: Line real objects (toy ducks, counters) up to match a told situation.
Replace them with linking cubes, then stand a drawn bar alongside the cubes.
Compare: 'What's the same between the cubes and the bar? What's different?'
Push the two groups together under one bar to show the whole being made of parts.
activities.insight: The bar/picture is an abstraction OF the real objects, not a decoration — and the two parts combine into one whole (part-part-whole), not two unrelated piles.

activities.title: Talk it through with a story partner
steps: Listen to a partner (an adult, peer, or in-role puppet) tell a story and build it with cubes.
Answer 'where's the 5 in your cubes? which bit is the 2? what happened to make it the whole group?'
When the partner builds a model, say what story it could be — keeping the exact numbers in.
In pairs, one child moves the cubes while the other draws/records, talking the mapping aloud.
activities.insight: Naming what each quantity refers to, and the action that joins them, keeps the numbers attached to meaning; saying it aloud makes the concrete→pictorial mapping explicit.

activities.title: Worked example: the pond scene (scaffold)
steps: Look at a fixed pond scene; reveal '5' over the ducks already there and '2' over the arrivals.
Open a flap to see the matching sentence 5 + 2 = 7.
Talk about which part of the picture each number stands for before moving to building your own.
activities.insight: In this described situation the joining action points to addition, shown here as 5 + 2 = 7 (other true sentences such as 2 + 5 = 7 or 7 = 5 + 2 describe the same relationship), and each number refers to a specific group in the scene; note that a static set of cubes, by contrast, could tell several stories (as in 'flip it').

checkQuestion: I'll tell you a story: 5 ducks are on the pond, and 2 more ducks swim up to join them. Show me this story with the cubes. Now point to the part of your cubes that is the 5, point to the part that is the 2, and show me the whole group of ducks. How do your cubes tell the same story as my words?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child mapping each quantity to its referent (5 = ducks already there, 2 = ducks that came) AND showing the joining action that makes the whole group, so the cubes are read as a relationship (parts making a whole), not two separate piles.
